newsitem.title: UK: ISO sees sharply reduced 96/97 world sugar surplus.
newsitem.headline: ISO sees sharply reduced 96/97 world sugar surplus.

text.p: The world sugar surplus should total 2.87 million tonnes raw value in 1996/97, sharply reduced from the 5.95 million reported for 1995/96, the International Sugar Organization (ISO) said on Wednesday.
End 1996/97 sugar stocks would total 40.92 million tonnes, after 34.02 million in 1995/96, the ISO said.

It recently revised downwards its estimate for 1996/97 production to 123.49 million tonnes based on the crop year from October to September. World production reached 123.95 million tonnes in the previous crop year, it said.
The expected cumulative addition to stocks of 8.8 million tonnes over two crop cycles had to exert considerable downward pressure on prices, the ISO said.
World sugar consumption was expected to total 123.49 million tonnes in 1996/97, slightly down from the previous 123.95 million tonnes.

Stocks, expressed in terms of a percentage ratio of consumption, would reach 33.9 percent after 28.8 percent in 1995/96, the ISO said. With the constant pressure from overhanging supply, world prices for raw sugar should approach their long-term average of 10 cents/lb while whites could fall to as low as 12.5 cents/lb.

Of the world's major producers, Australia was expected to turn out 5.80 million tonnes in 1996/97, after a previous 5.35 million, while Brazilian production would reach 13.50 million compared with 14.53 million in 1995/96. India, where most of the world's immense surplus is locked up, would produce 16.30 million tonnes of sugar in 1996/97, down from 17.67 million in 1995/96, the ISO said.
The 15-nation European Union, which dominates global beet sugar production, was expected to produce 17.20 million tonnes versus 16.95 million in 1995/96.
Production in Thailand, another significant exporter, would amount to 6.63 million tonnes after 6.38 million.
Cuba was expected to continue its crop recovery into 1996/97 and produce 5.05 million tonnes compared with 4.64 million tonnes in 1995/96, the ISO said.
